title: Dyāvāpṛthivī as Father and Mother, and Their Son
synthesis:
Five verses in jagatī, and the second of two hymns the same ṛṣi gives back to back to the pair — [[1.159]] stands immediately before it. What the hymn actually wants is held back until the last verse; the first four are spent establishing who is being asked.

*Te hi dyāvāpṛthivī* — these two. {{dyāvāpṛthivī}} is one word in the Sanskrit, a dual compound, and the epithets come in pairs: *viśvaśambhuvā*, bringing wellbeing to everything; *ṛtāvarī*, holding to {{ṛta}}; *dhārayatkavī*, holding up and seeing at once, so that what sustains the world also understands it; *sujanmanī*, of good birth. And *dhiṣaṇe*, a dual the tradition reads as the two world-halves themselves. Between them {{sūrya}} travels, *śuci*, pure, *dharmaṇā*, by the ordinance laid on him. The pair are not scenery for that journey. They are the frame within which anything at all can keep to a law.

The second verse names them plainly. *Uruvyacasā*, wide-reaching; *mahinī*, great; *asaścatā*, never failing — and then *pitā mātā ca*, father and mother, who guard the *bhuvanāni*, the worlds. They are *sudhṛṣṭame*, very bold, and *vapuṣye*, worth the sight, and the reason given is that the father clothed everything *rūpaiḥ*, with forms. Being visible is itself something done for us.

The third verse produces a son and refuses to name him. *Sa vahniḥ putraḥ pitroḥ* — that bearer, son of the two parents, *pavitravān*, possessed of the straining-cloth, *dhīra*, steady and skilled, and he cleanses the worlds *māyayā*, by the power that makes things be. Then he milks out, day after day, the bright *payas* — from *pṛśni*, the dappled cow, and from the bull of good seed. He draws from both parents at once, and the milk is one.

The fourth verse turns the generation around. *Ayaṃ devānām apasāṃ apastamaḥ* — among the gods who work, this one works most: he begot the two world-halves that bring good to all, he measured out the two *rajasī* with *sukratūyā*, effective skill, and he propped them apart with *ajarebhiḥ skambhanebhiḥ*, pillars that do not age. The son of verse 3 is the maker of his own parents in verse 4, and the hymn sets the two statements side by side without a word of reconciliation. *Viśvaśambhuvā* is repeated from the first verse, so the pair he made are exactly the pair the hymn opened by praising.

Then the fifth verse asks, and what it asks for is unexpectedly ordinary. *Te no gṛṇāne mahinī* — you two, being praised, great ones — *mahi śravaḥ kṣatraṃ dhāsathaḥ bṛhat*: set in us great renown and wide *kṣatra*, the capacity to rule. And the purpose: *yenābhi kṛṣṭīs tatanāma viśvahā*, by which we may extend over the peoples through all days. The verb is *tan*, to stretch — the same stretching by which the two world-halves were measured out in the verse before. Finally *sam invatam*, send us together *ojaḥ panāyyam*, strength worth praising. After four verses on the widest thing that exists, a household asks the world's parents for room to grow into, and asks it in their own vocabulary.
practice:
Heaven and earth as a married pair, addressed as one, is among the oldest things the tradition says, and it has never stopped saying it. The Anukramaṇī gives eleven sūktas across the whole Ṛgveda to *dyāvāpṛthivyau*, and three of the eleven are here in maṇḍala 1 — [[1.159]] and this one, consecutive, and [[1.185]] near the very close. Nothing in the collection is invoked more casually and hymned less often: the pair turn up in a line of half the hymns in the book and receive a sūkta of their own about once every hundred.

The order this hymn uses is the order still recited. *Dyauḥ* first, then *pṛthivī*, then what lies between them — the sequence of the śānti-pāṭha that closes so much daily recitation, where peace is invoked on the sky, then on the *antarikṣa*, then on the earth. And the epithet in verse 1 is worth keeping: *ṛtāvarī*, applied to heaven and earth themselves. Ṛta is not laid on them by a legislator from somewhere else. They hold it; that is what they are for.

Verse 2's *pitā mātā ca* is the phrase that survived. A Hindu who has ever said *dyauṣ pitā pṛthivī mātā* is saying what this verse says, and the reason given for calling them parents is not sentiment but function — *bhuvanāni rakṣataḥ*, they guard the worlds. Parenthood here is defined as keeping something else safe while it grows.

What the hymn finally asks for is the part to sit with. Not release, not vision, not even *rayi*. It asks for *śravas* and *kṣatra* — a name that carries and the standing to act among people — so that the family may *tan*, stretch, across the *kṛṣṭī*, the settled peoples. The verb is the one used two verses earlier for the measuring out of the worlds themselves. A householder asking to extend over the peoples is asking, in the hymn's own word, to do a small version of what heaven and earth were made by.
disagreements:
Verse 1 divides on two words. *Dhiṣaṇe* is given by the morphology simply as a dual for heaven and earth; Griffith prints "Two Bowls of noble kind," importing a vessel-image the word may or may not carry, and Wilson does not render it at all. The same verse's *rajaso dhārayatkavī* splits them further: Wilson reads *rajas* as the region of the rains and gets "able to sustain the water (of the rains)," while Griffith keeps it spatial — "sustainers of the region, Holy Ones and wise."

The son of verse 3 is unnamed in the text and unsettled in the reading. Sāyaṇa offers two possibilities without deciding: *vahni* is fire, that is Agni; or it is Āditya, the sun, of whom *vahni* is an epithet in the sense *phalasya voḍhā*, the bearer of the fruit of pious rites. Wilson prints the second — "the bearer (of rewards)" — while Griffith turns him into an officiant, "he the Priest with power to cleanse." Both readings survive the verse, because everything predicated of him (purifying, straining, milking the sky) fits either.

Verse 2's *vapuṣye na* also parts them: Wilson supplies a purpose, "as if (for the good) of embodied (beings)"; Griffith takes it as plain description, "the spirited, the beautiful."
note: dyāvāpṛthivyau ascription counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (11 sūktas); viśvaśambhuvā verified as recurring at v1 and v4 in the padapāṭha; dhiṣaṇe morphology from the grammar file
